meta.title: The Warning in the Kitchen
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses tone shift: the writer moves from calm instruction to a warning.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 115w at FK 7.4, part_2 109w at FK 5.6, part_3 96w at FK 6.9. The load is tone shift: the writer moves from calm instruction to a warning.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Isabella Beeton, The Book of Household Management (1861), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Beeton, Isabella. The Book of Household Management. 1861. Project Gutenberg eBook #10136, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10136, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Extracted a single 361-word passage and removed the paragraph number; the authoring pass will split long sentences and drop rare words; no facts added.
source.survey: A household manual explains why fruit is preserved and how it should be picked and stored, then how long boiling thickens the syrup, and ends with a sharp caution about the fire.

session.difficulty_basis: tone shift: the writer moves from calm instruction to a warning

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Fruit is a key item for health. The food lover can hardly have any treats without it. So, since it is so valuable, when we cannot have it fresh, we must keep it. It has long been a goal to keep fruit by some cheap method, but by one that would still keep it fit for cooking uses, like making tarts and other similar dishes. The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem; for, unless the sugar is used in large amounts, success is very uncertain. Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits: those kept this way are mainly meant for dessert.
passage.part_2: Fruit you plan to keep should be gathered in the morning, in dry weather, with the morning sun on it if possible. It will then have its fullest flavour and stay good longer than fruit gathered at any other time. Until fruit can be used, put it in the dairy, an ice-house, or the fridge. In an icehouse it will remain fresh and plump for several days. Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam. The fruit is the first and biggest part of making jam. Next comes the syrup the fruit will sit in, and this needs much care.
passage.part_3: In the candy maker's art, it is very important to measure the strength of the syrup exactly for each case. They know this by signs, and express it by certain technical terms. But to tell these apart properly requires very great attention and much practice. The main thing to know is that, as the syrup boils longer, its water will boil away, and it will become thicker. Great care must be taken in controlling the fire, so that the syrup does not boil over. The boiling is not carried so far as to burn the sugar.

items.prompt: What two problems does the writer say sugar causes when it is used to keep fruit?

tutor_only.confirm: Sugar is costly, and it destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentences 'The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem' and 'Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits' state both problems directly.
tutor_only.tell: Sugar costs a lot, so keeping fruit that way is a serious problem. Sugar is too strong and destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
help: Sugar costs a lot, so keeping fruit that way is a serious problem.
Sugar is too strong and destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
tutor_only.core_idea: Sugar costs a lot and it destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
accept_ideas: the cost of sugar is a serious problem
sugar is expensive so keeping fruit that way costs too much
sugar destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits
sugar is too strong for the taste people want in fruit
unless a lot of sugar is used, success is very uncertain
not_required: that sugared fruit is mainly for dessert
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say sugar keeps fruit fresh and plump for several days.
if_they_say.ask: Which part of the passage says that, and does it talk about sugar?

items.prompt: The passage says sugar is costly and must be used in large amounts. It also says sugar destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits. What do these two facts together show about keeping fruit with sugar?

tutor_only.confirm: Together they show that keeping fruit with sugar is a serious problem for cooking uses.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The answer comes from the sentences 'The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem; for, unless the sugar is used in large amounts, success is very uncertain' and 'Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits.' The first gives the cost and uncertainty; the second gives the taste damage.
tutor_only.tell: Sugar costs a lot and must be used in large amounts. It also ruins the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
help: The cost sentence says sugar is a serious problem. The taste sentence says sugar destroys a wanted flavour.
Connect the problem of cost with the problem of ruined taste.
tutor_only.core_idea: Keeping fruit with sugar has both a cost problem and a taste problem, so it is not a good method for fruit wanted for cooking.
accept_ideas: Keeping fruit with sugar is costly and can fail unless much sugar is used.
Sugar can destroy the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
Sugar preservation is a serious problem for fruit meant for cooking.
The two facts show sugar keeping has cost and taste drawbacks.
not_required: A list of all preservation methods
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say sugar keeping is cheap and always works.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence says the cost is a serious problem and success is uncertain?

items.prompt: What can you conclude about fruit picked in wet or foggy weather if you plan to make jam?

tutor_only.confirm: Fruit picked in wet or foggy weather will mildew and cannot be used for jam.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part 2 says, 'Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam.'
tutor_only.tell: Wet or foggy weather makes fruit mildew soon. Such fruit will not work for jam.
help: Think about what happens to fruit in wet or foggy weather.
Use the line about mildew and jam.
tutor_only.core_idea: Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather is unfit for jam because it mildews.
accept_ideas: It will mildew and be no use for jam.
Wet or foggy weather makes the fruit spoil and become unusable for jam.
The fruit is a bad choice for jam because it will mildew.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say wet fruit is still fine for jam if washed.
if_they_say.ask: What does part_2 say happens to fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather?

items.prompt: Wet fruit 'will soon mildew and be no use for jam.' What does that warning make you feel?

tutor_only.confirm: It makes wet weather feel risky, not just inconvenient.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The warning is in the sentence 'Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam.' The words 'soon mildew' and 'no use' create a cautious, warned feeling.
tutor_only.tell: The phrase 'will soon mildew and be no use for jam' sounds like a warning. It makes wet weather feel like a threat to the fruit.
help: Read the sentence about wet or foggy weather. Notice the words 'soon mildew' and 'no use.'
Think about how those words make the dry-weather rule feel more serious.
tutor_only.core_idea: The warning phrase makes the reader feel cautious about wet weather because it threatens the fruit with mildew and ruin.
accept_ideas: The warning makes wet weather feel risky or threatening.
It makes the reader cautious about picking fruit at the wrong time.
It makes the dry-weather rule feel serious.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.ask: What feeling does the warning phrase create for the reader?

items.prompt: How does the writer's plan change from broad reasons to exact syrup steps?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer starts with broad reasons and problems, then moves to exact syrup signs and fire cautions.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part 1 gives broad reasons fruit is valuable and sugar is costly or uncertain. Part 3 gives exact syrup signs, careful measuring, and fire control so syrup does not boil over or burn.
tutor_only.tell: The opening gives broad reasons and sugar problems; the last part gives exact syrup signs and fire cautions. The writer moves from why fruit matters to how to judge and control boiling syrup.
help: Part 1 spends time on why fruit is valuable and why sugar is a problem.
Part 3 spends time on measuring syrup by signs and controlling the fire.
tutor_only.core_idea: The writer starts with broad reasons and problems about keeping fruit, then shifts to precise syrup-making signs and cautions.
accept_ideas: Part 1 gives general reasons and sugar problems; part 3 gives exact syrup signs and fire cautions.
The writing changes from background about fruit and sugar to careful process steps and warnings.
It moves from explaining why fruit must be kept to telling how to judge and control boiling syrup.
not_required: quoting the technical terms for syrup
retelling all three parts in order
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.
